text:
Green technologies are mineral-intensive: electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and grids need cobalt, lithium, copper, manganese, graphite and rare earths. The International Energy Agency estimates that electric cars require six times more minerals than a petrol or diesel car. A wind power plant requires about nine times more minerals than a gas-fired plant.

As the global green transition speeds up, the growing demand for green technologies and minerals creates an opening for Africa, which has deposits of several of the minerals needed.

Read more: Zimbabwe’s lithium is in demand for making batteries: how to make sure benefits flow to the local economy

Yet just having these minerals in the ground does not automatically create industries or shared prosperity. In fact, developing countries endowed with minerals often struggle to benefit economically from mining.

We are scholars of how countries build industries and reshape their economies. Our latest study, commissioned by the World Bank, explored how far African countries have moved beyond mining the minerals needed for the energy transition. We examined whether they are processing and refining these minerals or making components for green technologies that use them.

Our analysis followed four steps. First, we identified the transition minerals found in each African country. Second, we examined trade data to see which countries export these minerals and where they are sold.

Third, we looked at where African countries participate in the value chain of green technology. We wanted to find out whether they only mine the mineral and then export it raw, or whether they process it before selling it or produce a final product for sale, such as solar panels. Fourth, we reviewed national and regional mineral and industrial policies.

Read more: A new class of metals could transform Africa’s clean energy economy – scientists explain

We found that African countries have deposits of 41 minerals that are used across bioenergy, electricity networks and infrastructure, batteries, energy storage and electric vehicles, and carbon capture and storage. These minerals are also sought after for fuel cells and hydrogen, geothermal energy, heat pumps, hydropower, nuclear power, solar power and wind power.

However, most African countries still export transition minerals in raw or lightly processed form rather than turning them into higher-value materials, components and finished products.

Read more: Has finance for green industry had an impact in Africa? What’s happened in 41 countries over 20 years

African countries therefore have only a very small presence in the green-technology industries that depend on these minerals. As a result, Africa’s mineral wealth has not yet led to high levels of industrial activity, well-paid jobs, higher incomes or wide improvements in living standards.

We found that national and regional institutions are taking steps to change this, but most initiatives are still at an early stage.

Collective mineral strength, shallow value capture

Our research found deposits, reserves, or production of at least one transition mineral in 48 African countries. South Africa had 24 of the 41 minerals; Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) each had 14.

Collectively, Africa holds about 96% of global platinum group metal reserves, 77% of phosphate reserves, and 55% of cobalt reserves. Phosphate and cobalt are used in electric vehicle batteries, while platinum is used in technologies that produce and use green hydrogen.

Yet most countries individually accounted for only small global shares. This matters because small national volumes can make it harder for a country acting alone to influence buyers, attract large processing plants, build complete supply chains or compete with established producers elsewhere.

Read more: DRC is the world’s largest producer of cobalt – how control by local elites can shape the global battery industry

Trade data reinforces these findings. Notably, apart from South Africa, Nigeria and the DRC, most African countries exported less than 1% of each mineral globally. For several minerals, such as nickel, rare earths, silver and lithium, Africa’s five largest exporters together supplied less than 10% of world exports.

African countries could strengthen their position in mineral markets by coordinating their trade policies rather than acting separately. Private companies hold mining licences, but permission to extract minerals does not always include an unrestricted right to export them. Governments may therefore have some scope to coordinate trade rules. How this would work alongside companies’ existing rights, and whether it would require their agreement, needs to be further studied.

Read more: Lithium in the Sahel: how armed groups are exploiting the global scramble for the critical mineral

A deeper weakness identified in our study is limited local processing of minerals. This mainly happens in a few countries such as South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The processing these countries do often involves crushing and concentrating ore, rather than making products from the mineral.

African countries lose out because of this. For example, Congolese cobalt can sell for US$5.80 per kilogram at the point of extraction. But after local refining, the price increases to US$16.20 per kilogram, nearly tripling its value.

A green economy built on old dependencies

Asia (China in particular) is the leading importer of 16 minerals from Africa. It imported over 30% of those exports on average, and was the second biggest buyer of six other green transition minerals.

Our research found that China absorbed over 40% of Africa’s annual mineral ore exports. This shows that Africa is repeating a familiar pattern: mining raw materials while other countries turn them into more valuable products.

Read more: China and the US are in a race for critical minerals. African countries need to make the rules

The history of Africa, plus low industrialisation levels, means that African countries are also almost invisible in green technology value chains. Between 2017 and 2023, Africa’s global patent share across the technologies studied remained below 0.4%, while its export share was below 1% in every category. African countries currently participate in the green economy more as consumers, rather than producers.

African governments are asserting agency

We also found that African governments are changing mining laws, restricting exports, taking ownership stakes and forming partnerships to gain more from their minerals. They want more processing, investment, jobs and income to stay at home. Most are acting individually, although some are working together across borders.

Acting alone has limits. Many countries supply too little to influence large international buyers. If one country demands higher prices or local processing, buyers can shop elsewhere.

Many also lack reliable electricity, affordable loans, transport and skilled workers to process minerals and make components.

What needs to happen next

Africa is very strong in minerals as a continent. However, deeper regional cooperation would help African countries build industries, not simply trade more easily with one another, a central thesis of a related study, Integrating Africa: From Threads to Hubs. Pooling mineral supplies, markets, infrastructure and skills could lower costs and give them more power when negotiating with global companies. A shared processing centre serving countries across Africa would also help the continent.

Read more: Why Africa needs a green bank to fund climate action and build its own renewable technology

To make this happen, African finance and mineral institutions and national governments must agree on common priorities and similar rules about how minerals are processed, and how environmental damage is managed.

Development finance has a role to play. Regional development banks and other African financiers could help fund shared electricity, transport and mineral-processing infrastructure, while universities and businesses develop the technical skills these industries need.

Partnerships with foreign governments and companies should also go beyond extracting and exporting minerals. They should include commitments to process more minerals in Africa, share technology and know-how, train workers, and help local firms become suppliers to emerging green industries.

title: Your Next General Motors EV Could Run Batteries With Fully Recycled Cathode Material
description:

The pathway to using fully recycled cathode material took years to build.
It has to be refined into active cathode material, namely the layer of the battery cell whose nickel, cobalt, and manganese content drives cost, performance, and safety.
The refinement process resulted in more than 12 metric tons (26,455 pounds) of new active cathode material.
Testing showed that cells built from the recycled material performed as well as cells made from new stock.
text:
Detroit's largest automaker has confirmed that its battery-electric vehicles now ship with traction batteries that may contain 100 percent recycled nickel, cobalt, and manganese. This cathode material comes from battery packs originating from older BEVs. The first vehicles produced with such batteries rolled off the assembly lines at Spring Hill Assembly and Factory ZERO earlier this month.

The pathway to using fully recycled cathode material took years to build. General Motors collaborated with partners across cell manufacturing, materials processing, and the recycling side of the biz to recover critical minerals from retired packs and return them to completely new cells. The roster includes LG Energy Solution, Ultium Cells, and Cirba Solutions.

As per the largest automaker of the Detroit Big Three, no fewer than 80 end-of-life batteries were recovered by Cirba Solutions. After disassembly, the packs were then processed, converting their contents into a black mass containing the cathode and anode materials. That mass cannot be used on its own.

It has to be refined into active cathode material, namely the layer of the battery cell whose nickel, cobalt, and manganese content drives cost, performance, and safety. The refinement process resulted in more than 12 metric tons (26,455 pounds) of new active cathode material. Before any of it went into a cell, it had to clear the same quality, performance, and safety validation GM applies to virgin material.

Testing showed that cells built from the recycled material performed as well as cells made from new stock. Ultium Cells, namely the GM joint venture with LG Energy Solution, then produced the cells. Workers ultimately assembled them into all-new modules and packs at the Spring Hill and Factory ZERO plants.

Raw materials are among the largest cost drivers in a battery cell in the automotive industry, so recovering them can push cell costs down over time while cutting reliance on newly mined material. Shoring up the supply chains also needs to be considered. GM claims that current recycling processes can recover up to 95 percent of the nickel, cobalt, and manganese in an end-of-line pack.

Depending on process conditions and chemistry, up to 80 percent of the lithium can be recovered as well. Future processes are certain to push those numbers higher. All told, more than 70 percent of battery components are recycled. Packs can also move into stationary energy storage before they're torn down for materials.

GM and Redwood Materials are deploying no fewer than 10,000 second-life batteries into energy infrastructure, including the largest second-life battery microgrid in North America. Additional deployments are planned inside the automaker's US manufacturing footprint, and General Motors isn't alone in chasing this.

Both Tesla and Porsche are betting on battery recycling, and we also have to remember that Rivian is working with Redwood Materials to run its Illinois-based factory on second-life battery storage. For General Motors, the pilot's real output is data. Partners involved in the program expect nearly 14 million electric vehicle batteries reaching end-of-life status by 2040.

Given how many batteries will hit end of life over the next decade and beyond, General Motors' program gives the company a foundation of experience to build on as volumes grow. The pilot supports larger goals of cutting the carbon footprint of battery materials and reducing costs to consumers, with more details to be shared by GM at Climate Week NYC.

title: France's Cleantech Funding Boom: €1.4 Billion Signals a Market Moving Toward Scale

text:
France’s cleantech sector is gaining momentum as investors and public institutions support decarbonisation, renewable energy, resource efficiency and sustainable technologies, strengthening the country’s low-carbon industrial ecosystem.

France’s cleantech sector is attracting strong investment as companies, investors and public institutions increase spending on decarbonisation, energy security, renewable energy and resource efficiency. French cleantech companies raised €1.4 billion (US$1.64 billion) during the first half of 2026, comprising €830 million (US$971 million) in private equity and €565 million (US$661 million) through debt, grants, guarantees and loans. Government support accounted for €215 million (US$252 million) of the funding, highlighting the role of public finance in accelerating emerging technologies.

Energy was the largest investment category, representing 39% of total funding, equivalent to approximately €546 million ( US$639 million). Resources and environmental management accounted for 21%, or around €294 million (US$344 million), while agriculture and food represented 19%, equivalent to approximately €266 million (US$311 million). The funding mix is significant because cleantech businesses often require substantial upfront capital for technology development, demonstration projects, manufacturing facilities and infrastructure before reaching commercial scale. The growing availability of private equity alongside government grants, loans and guarantees is helping companies move from early-stage development toward industrial deployment. The investment momentum also reflects France’s broader push to strengthen low-carbon infrastructure and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.

The key challenge now is converting this capital into commercial projects, manufacturing capacity, revenues, employment and export opportunities, determining how effectively France can build a competitive domestic cleantech industry.

Energy Emerges as the Largest Investment Segment

Energy emerged as the largest investment segment in France’s cleantech sector during H1 2026, accounting for 39% of total funding. Based on the €1.4 billion raised across the sector, this represents approximately €546 million ( US$639 million) directed toward energy-related technologies. Resources and environmental management accounted for 21%, while agriculture and food represented 19%. Energy investment spans multiple technologies, including renewable power generation, energy storage, smart grids, energy-efficiency solutions, low-carbon fuels and advanced nuclear technologies.

The diversity of these investments reflects France’s need to expand low-carbon electricity capacity while supporting the electrification and decarbonisation of industry and transport. Innovative nuclear technology is also attracting substantial capital, with approximately €165 million (US$193 million) in private funding during H1 2026, according to Cleantech for France. This highlights the distinctive structure of France’s energy-transition market, where investment is distributed across both established and emerging low-carbon technologies rather than concentrated in renewables alone.

The combination of renewable energy, nuclear power, storage and grid technologies is creating opportunities across the wider energy ecosystem, from electricity generation and transmission to energy management, infrastructure development and industrial decarbonisation.

Market Stats

Energy accounted for 39% of France’s €1.4 billion ( US$1.64 billion) cleantech funding in H1 2026, making it the largest investment category.

Energy attracted approximately €330 million (US$386 million) in private-equity investment, representing nearly 40% of total private-equity funding.

Innovative nuclear energy attracted approximately €165 million (US$193 million) in private funding during H1 2026, including fundraising by Calogena, Jimmy and newcleo.

France’s France 2030 programme allocated more than €180 million (US$211 million) to its first two innovative small-reactor projects announced in March 2026.

France has committed approximately €1.2 billion (US$1.40 billion) through France 2030 to support the development of its nuclear sector, including innovative small-reactor technologies.

Government Funding Is Shaping Commercialization

Government support is playing a significant role in the development of the French cleantech market. Of the €565 million (US$661 million) raised through debt, grants, guarantees and loans during H1 2026, €215 million (US$252 million) came from government grants. Public funding is particularly relevant to capital-intensive technologies because it can reduce the financial risk associated with demonstration and industrialisation. This is important in areas such as renewable infrastructure, hydrogen, batteries, carbon-management technologies and industrial decarbonisation, where commercial projects can require substantial upfront investment.

France also has an established public investment ecosystem through Bpifrance. Its cleantech, smart-city and impact funds have almost €300 million (US$351 million) under management and can invest between €500,000 (US$585,000) and €10 million (US$11.7 million) in Series A to Series C financing alongside private investors. Its portfolio includes companies working in smart mobility, renewable energy, smart grids, green chemistry, agritech, circular economy and smart buildings.

Another important instrument is Bpifrance’s SPI industrialisation fund, which manages approximately €800 million ( US$936 million), with individual investments ranging from €10 million ( US$11.7 million) to €160 million (US$187 million). Such public investment can help cleantech companies overcome the “valley of death” between prototype development and mass production by providing capital for manufacturing capacity and industrial-scale deployment.

Investment Is Spread Across Multiple Cleantech Segments

Although energy captures the largest share, France's cleantech market is increasingly diversified. Resources and environmental management account for 21% of investment, while agriculture and food represent 19%.

This creates several distinct market opportunities.

Circular economy and resource management can include recycling, waste treatment, material recovery and eco-design. Increasing pressure to reduce raw-material consumption can create demand for technologies that improve material efficiency.

Agritech and sustainable food technologies represent another important opportunity. Companies are developing solutions aimed at improving agricultural productivity while reducing environmental impacts and resource consumption.

Mobility is also developing as a cleantech investment category. In September 2026, VINCI Concessions, Epopee Gestion and Ademe Investissement mobilized €90 million (US$105 million) for an initial rollout of 20 high-power charging stations for electric heavy goods vehicles in France and Europe. The stations are designed around high-power and Megawatt Charging System technology for electric freight vehicles.

Meanwhile, France is also investing in floating offshore wind infrastructure. In July 2026, the government announced €260 million (US$304 million) in public funding for floating-wind infrastructure at five French ports, with total investment across those ports expected to approach €1.17 billion (US$1.37 billion).

These developments show that the cleantech opportunity extends beyond startups developing individual technologies. Infrastructure, logistics, industrial equipment and enabling technologies can also capture significant investment.

Competitive Landscape: Who Is Capturing the Capital?

France's cleantech competitive landscape includes startups, industrial corporations, utilities, infrastructure companies, financial investors and government-backed institutions.

Bpifrance currently reports a cleantech, smart-city and impact portfolio containing 25 technology and service startups. Its portfolio companies have raised more than €450 million (US$512.6 million) from international financial and corporate investors, demonstrating how public investment can help attract additional private capital.

At the larger end of the market, established companies are also becoming important participants in the transition. Industrial corporations have the financial resources, manufacturing infrastructure and customer relationships needed to commercialize technologies at scale.

This creates a competitive environment with several layers:

Startups compete through technological innovation.

Growth-stage companies compete on commercialization and scaling.

Industrial companies leverage manufacturing and distribution capabilities.

Energy companies provide infrastructure and project-development expertise.

Financial investors determine which technologies receive growth capital.

Government institutions influence market development through grants, guarantees and strategic investment.

For market researchers, mapping these participants is critical. A competitive landscape should track funding rounds, technology focus, partnerships, patents, production capacity, customer contracts and geographic expansion, rather than relying solely on company valuations.

The Market Is Moving from Innovation Toward Industrial Scale

The biggest question facing the French cleantech market is whether €1.4 billion (US$1.59 billion) of financing can translate into commercially viable businesses and large-scale infrastructure.

This transition is particularly important for physical technologies. A startup can demonstrate a working battery, electrolyser, carbon-capture system or renewable-energy component, but scaling production requires factories, equipment, skilled workers, supply chains and long-term customers.

Bpifrance's industrialization strategy explicitly targets this challenge. Its SPI fund focuses on projects requiring significant capital and facing technology, industrial and commercial risks, with the objective of transforming innovative technologies into industrial activity and employment.

The European funding environment is also supporting this transition. In March 2026, the European Commission awarded €2.7 billion (US$3.08 billion) to 54 clean-industry projects across 17 countries and 17 industrial sectors through the Innovation Fund. The projects cover renewable energy, manufacturing, refineries, cement and lime, and net-zero mobility.

For French companies, access to both national and European financing can potentially expand the capital available for industrial-scale projects.

Key Risks and Market Challenges

Despite strong funding activity, the market faces several risks.

The first is capital intensity. Companies may require hundreds of millions of euros to move from pilot projects to commercial production.

The second is technology risk. A technology that works successfully at laboratory or pilot scale may not necessarily achieve competitive economics at industrial scale.

Third, regulatory uncertainty can affect project timelines and investment decisions.

Fourth, companies face supply-chain risks, particularly where technologies depend on critical minerals, specialized components or imported equipment.

Finally, increasing competition means French companies must compete not only domestically but also with companies from the United States, China, Germany and other European markets.

Unlock exclusive market insights. Blog news—Download the Brochure now and dive deeper into the future of the Market

Future Outlook

France’s cleantech sector is expected to maintain strong growth as government policies, private investment and industrial demand accelerate the transition toward a low-carbon economy. Future opportunities are expected to emerge across renewable energy, nuclear technologies, energy storage, smart grids, sustainable mobility, circular economy and green industrial processes. Increasing demand for energy security and reduced fossil-fuel dependence could support continued investment in clean infrastructure and enabling technologies. Public funding is also expected to remain important in supporting emerging technologies move from demonstration to commercial-scale deployment. The sector’s long-term development will depend on converting investment into manufacturing capacity, commercially viable projects, skilled employment and stronger export opportunities.

authors: Emily Jones, For WABE, Courtesy Georgia Power Company
description:

For new natural gas plants, utilities would need to either install carbon capture or simply run the plants less often.
In their lawsuit, groups including the Natural Resources Defense Council and American Public Health Association argue the proposed change threatens public health and the environment.
Georgia's emissions future Georgia Power continues to use its two coal plants, plus power from Plant Gaston in Alabama.
This article originally appeared on Savannah Morning News: Georgia emissions could rise after EPA rule repeal Reporting by Emily Jones, For WABE / Savannah Morning News USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Reuters_USATLocal_GANews
text:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.

As environmental and public health groups challenge a Trump administration proposal to repeal climate-related standards for power plants, advocates in Georgia warn the rollback is likely to increase greenhouse gas emissions in the state.

The rule the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency wants to repeal was finalized during the Biden Administration. It gives existing coal plants the option to either use technology designed to capture carbon emissions or to close entirely, with a deadline of 2032 to comply. For new natural gas plants, utilities would need to either install carbon capture or simply run the plants less often.

In a statement announcing the change, the EPA said it will "unleash the full potential of America's vast energy resources, including coal and natural gas."

"The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on," said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in the statement.

In their lawsuit, groups including the Natural Resources Defense Council and American Public Health Association argue the proposed change threatens public health and the environment.

"Clean air is a basic human right. Power plant pollution threatens the health of millions of Americans and fuels climate change, worsening extreme heat, poor air quality, and other serious health risks," said Georges C. Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association, in a statement.

Retiring, then extending coal

In Georgia, where Georgia Power currently operates two coal-fired power plants, the Biden-era rule, which most experts agree was geared toward phasing out coal by requiring either costly technology or closure, was starting to have an effect.

In its 2022 long-term plan, Georgia Power, the state's largest electricity utility, determined that it was too expensive to keep its coal plants running with carbon capture systems. At the time, it had three coal plants in operation in Georgia, plus units at a plant in Alabama that use coal as a backup. The utility asked for permission from state regulators to retire the entire fleet of coal plants, and ultimately got approval to close all but one: Plant Bowen, in Bartow County.

When Trump came back into office, though, the calculus changed. According to Maggie Shober of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, utilities have been planning for the repeal of the Biden-era rule since President Donald Trump was elected to a second term.

"Everybody understood it was not going to stay in effect," she said.

Indeed, in 2025, Georgia Power got approval from the Georgia Public Service Commission to put off retiring two power plants - one of its own, and one operated by its sister company, Alabama Power. The agreement extended the life of one coal unit at Plant Scherer, near Macon, and four at Plant Gaston, in Alabama. Plant Gaston primarily runs on natural gas, with coal as a backup.

At the same time, the agreement also called for the company to pursue compliance with the Biden-era rule for Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer.

During hearings leading up to the decision, Georgia Power officials told the PSC that in order to account for the regulatory uncertainty, the company ran nine planning scenarios, three of which included compliance with the rule and six of which did not.

"These scenarios provide a flexible framework for the company to evaluate its options among differing plausible future scenarios, positioning it to make informed resource planning decisions," Jeff Grubb, the utility's director of resource policy and planning, said in his testimony at the hearing.

In 2024, the most recent year for which the U.S. Energy Information Administration has published data, Plant Bowen emitted nearly 11 million tons of carbon dioxide, and Plant Scherer emitted more than eight million tons, placing them in the top 25 of the most carbon-emitting power plants in the country. Plant Gaston emitted more than two million tons that year.

Georgia's emissions future

Georgia Power continues to use its two coal plants, plus power from Plant Gaston in Alabama. And, as a result of the rising demand from data centers, the utility is building out new capacity to generate power with natural gas, which is largely composed of methane.

Without the EPA restrictions, Shober said emissions from those new gas turbines could more than double. Under the Biden-era rule, the utility would have been able to run them about 40 percent of the time without adding expensive carbon-capture technology, producing about four million tons of carbon dioxide a year, according to Shober. Running 85 percent of the time, as they'd likely be able to do under normal operations if the EPA's proposed changes go through, she estimated the turbines would produce 8.5 million tons.

Georgia Power's parent company, Southern Company, did not grant an interview or answer specific questions. A spokesperson sent a statement saying the company "supports regulatory certainty with a durable framework that leads to reliable and affordable electricity for our customers." The statement made no mention of the company's greenhouse gas reduction goal of net zero by 2050.

The EPA's rule change isn't final yet. There will be a public comment period, plus the lawsuit challenging the change will have to move through the court system.

text:
A new Sierra Club analysis says that the nation's largest electric utilities are sliding backward on clean energy.

Rather than accelerating coal retirements and renewable development, many of these utilities are keeping dirty fuels in the mix and scaling back climate action promises.

These changes will be felt among the American public in the form of costlier power, more pollution, and increasing climate-related expenses.

Here's what to know

In the Sierra Club's latest Dirty Truth Report, it gave 76 of the country's biggest utilities an F and said 41% have pulled back from climate action goals in the last two years.

To score the companies, the group reviewed utility plans as of mid-2026 and focused on three areas: how fast coal plants are being retired, whether new gas plants are being added, and how quickly clean energy is expanding to replace fossil fuels and serve growing electricity demand.

"We studied the 50 parent companies that own the most fossil fuel generation, comprised of 76 operating companies, which collectively own half of all remaining coal and gas generation in the U.S. … The utilities studied scored 7/100, earning an F, worsening their overall score by 11 points since 2021," the Sierra Club summarized.

Across all three measures, the outlook was bleak. Utilities now project that only 25% of coal-fired generating capacity will close by the end of the decade, compared with 29% in 2025, 30% in 2024, and 35% in 2023. This is insufficient to protect Americans from the worst health and economic impacts of toxic air and climate change.

The utilities are also planning so much additional gas generation that it would equal roughly one-quarter of typical U.S. electricity demand, with much of that growth tied to expected AI data center demand.

"Utilities' lack of proactive planning contributed to the timing and cost pressures that utilities now cite as justifications to remain reliant on fossil fuels," the Sierra Club explained. "By delaying action, utilities wasted opportunities to capitalize on clean energy tax credits for the cheaper, cleaner energy needed to replace old, expensive coal plants and serve growing electricity demand."

More background

Because these companies control over half of the nation's coal and fossil gas generation fleet, their choices have a major impact on emissions, air pollution, and the speed at which cleaner energy infrastructure can be built.

By extending the life of coal plants and approving new gas facilities, utilities are saddling customers with years of fuel and maintenance spending that will be reflected in their power bills.

At the utility level, the clearest fixes are the same ones the Sierra Club used in its grading system: retire coal plants faster; stop building new gas capacity; and replace that generation with more solar, wind, and battery storage.

Residents can weigh in during public utility commission proceedings, support local and state policies that expand renewable energy, and ask hard questions when companies make climate promises that do not match their investment plans.

Where can I learn more?

These stories offer more details on the utility decisions and policy shifts reshaping the U.S. power mix.

• In Utah, a major utility made the disappointing step backward of keeping coal plants running.

• The Department of Energy ordered a shift toward fossil fuels that could slow cleaner power growth.

• Major energy companies are backing away from climate action commitments as fossil fuel expansion regains federal support.

text:
This investigation was reported in a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations.

MCDERMITT CALDERA, Ore.—On a cold and overcast spring morning, Katie Fite stood in one of the country’s last sage-grouse strongholds, contemplating the wooden stakes in the ground that she fears warn of its destruction.

Every spring, males of the chunky bird species with spiky tail feathers come to a dwindling number of locations to strut, pop their inflatable white neck pouches and make a “paloop, paloop” sound in an attempt to court a mate. As their name suggests, sage-grouse need sagebrush, the green-brown shrub that once dominated arid Western landscapes. But both the bird and its habitat are rapidly disappearing due to climate change, invasive species, wildfires and energy development.

Now a mining company wants to extract lithium here.

Millions of sage-grouse once filled the West, but federal data shows their numbers have plummeted 80 percent since 1965 as more than a million acres of the sagebrush landscape they depend on is lost every year. They’ve long teetered toward the endangered-species list.

“We want to save sage-grouse?” Fite, public lands director for WildLands Defense, asked as she walked through the mating area, known as a lek, on the public lands where the McDermitt Lithium project would dig. “This is not how we do it. This is a travesty.”

The project’s owner agreed to avoid drilling during the sage-grouse breeding season in an effort to avoid impacting a species that is easily put off mating if conditions aren’t just right. But there is so little sagebrush habitat left in the country, Fite said, that “you can’t even pretend to mitigate this.”

Today, the U.S. has only one operating lithium mine—Albemarle’s Silver Peak in Nevada. By 2030, at least six new mining projects are predicted to be extracting lithium from American soil and another 13 will soon follow, according to a database compiled by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News. Scores more are proposed, their wooden stakes marking companies’ claims.

This element of the energy transition—lithium is used in batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage—poses stark dilemmas in the communities atop the so-called white gold. Mining it uses and displaces water, and much of it is found in water-scarce regions. Tribal nations repeatedly harmed by past extraction are disproportionately located on or near lithium-rich lands.

And then there’s vulnerable wildlife. The McDermitt Caldera’s basin is rolling hills of sagebrush and rare native wildflowers growing on strangely yellow soils in an ancient volcanic depression on the Oregon-Nevada border, its springs providing a home to threatened Lahontan cutthroat trout just as its sagebrush sustains sage-grouse. Further south in Nevada, a fully approved lithium mine, Ioneer’s Rhyolite Ridge, has faced controversy over its siting at the world’s only location of an endangered buckwheat. And scores of other proposed projects are near vulnerable species in wild, intact landscapes.

President Donald Trump is both undercutting endangered-species protections and boosting the country’s domestic mining industry, leaving plants and animals in lithium areas particularly exposed. Though the Trump administration has abandoned U.S. climate efforts and attacked the energy transition, it’s streamlining and fast-tracking permitting for lithium mines whose demand rests on that shift.

The remote McDermitt Caldera could end up home to multiple such projects.

Some of the mining claims are for projects in very early stages. But Thacker Pass, a lithium mine permitted by the first Trump administration, is under construction on the Nevada side of the caldera. The McDermitt Lithium project that would mine the lek where Fite stood is one of the first mines to be fast-tracked during the second Trump term.

All told, the Trump administration approved fast-tracking for 10 lithium mines across the country since last year. It’s doing so under a 2015 law launching the FAST-41 program that streamlines permits for large infrastructure projects. But Trump officials created an outgrowth they’re calling the “transparency program” that skips a number of requirements under the law, including coordination with local governments.

The McDermitt Lithium project tried to get into FAST-41 in 2023 but was denied by the Biden administration, according to documents from the federal agency managing the program and obtained by Inside Climate News and CJI.

The project, owned by Australian mining company Jindalee’s subsidiary HiTech Minerals Inc., is a prime example of the administration’s push to quicken mining permitting across the board. Even before McDermitt Lithium made it into FAST-41, the federal Bureau of Land Management (BLM) gave the public just five days in March 2025 to comment on the company’s proposed exploratory drilling—one of the first steps in creating a new mine.

Public backlash forced the BLM to extend the comment period to 31 days, still far shorter than usual, and the project was then added to the fast-track program to further speed its way through permitting.

In December, the BLM approved Jindalee’s plan to drill at 168 sites and build 21.5 miles of access roads across 73 of the 7,200 acres of public land the project’s site encompasses. Now, the Oregon Natural Desert Association, Great Old Broads for Wilderness and Great Basin Resource Watch are suing the BLM over its project approval, alleging the agency failed to properly evaluate the mine’s environmental impacts to species like the sage-grouse.

“When they provided at first only a five-day comment period, they were certainly making it clear that they had no interest in what the public had to say, which is certainly an indication that perhaps they’re not conducting the kind of hard-look analysis that’s required [under the country’s environmental laws],” said Ryan Houston, the executive director of the Oregon Natural Desert Association.

Records of communications between BLM staffers obtained via a public records request by the Oregon Natural Desert Association and shared with Inside Climate News and CJI reveal regional staff were surprised by the project’s short comment period. The decision to limit the time for public input, they wrote, came from higher-ranking officials.

“Staff are ‘pausing’ their review of the HiTech [environmental assessment] and it will be completed at a higher level,” one staffer wrote in a message, adding that she was unsure how, with such a fast timeline, the agency would be able to incorporate the minimum reclamation requirements to restore the land after drilling is completed. “Seems it changes daily and keeps getting worse,” she added.

A different staffer asked, “How is that timeline allowed?”

Jindalee CEO Ian Rodger said in a statement to CJI and Inside Climate News that the company was pleased to be added to the fast-track list but was not aware of the decision to shorten the public comment process. He said Jindalee supported the decision to extend it.

The project is currently only conducting exploratory drilling, not yet digging a full-scale mine, Rodger added. He said the company is committed to continued community and tribal consultation. In April, Jindalee’s HiTech Minerals announced plans with Constellation Acquisition Corp. to form US Elemental Inc. and go public. Jindalee, which will retain majority ownership of HiTech, plans to support the BLM in its legal defense of the project.

Larisa Bogardus, a BLM spokesperson, said the agency determined it would be “beneficial” to extend the initial comment period after evaluating the first batch of public comments. The project’s fast-track inclusion does not predetermine the permitting process’ outcome, she added.

But the environmental groups’ lawsuit alleges the project’s fast tracking resulted in its permits not meeting the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act. The BLM only conducted an environmental assessment for the project, and not a more intensive impact review, which are required for more environmentally damaging projects and have been done for similar mineral exploration projects, Houston said.

That led to inadequacies in the review. The agency conducted no study on whether pumping 31.5 million gallons of groundwater would draw down the aquifer, harming local streams vital for wildlife. It evaluated only direct impacts to sage-grouse habitat, rather than the landscape affected across the project’s 7,200 acres. And it undertook no evaluation of the cumulative impacts lithium mining will have across the McDermitt Caldera.

Experts say mining in the U.S. could be done with fewer environmental impacts than if the nation relies on imports from other countries, where much of its current lithium supply originates. But rollbacks of both environmental protections and community engagement make that less likely, they say.

In August, Oregon’s mining regulator issued the final permits needed for the project’s exploratory drilling to commence, with no public comment period. Despite that, more than 8,000 people from Oregon and beyond sent letters to state officials opposing the permit.

The final permit requires Jindalee to meet certain conditions before proceeding, such as developing a plan with the state to mitigate impacts to sage-grouse and to coordinate with the Burns Paiute Tribe, one of the tribes concerned about the project.

Alex Lopez, a spokesperson for Oregon’s mining regulator, said in a statement that exploration permits do not require a public comment period and that compliance with permit conditions is evaluated over the project’s life by multiple agencies.

Before the project received approval to drill, the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife told the state mining regulator and BLM that it has serious concerns about the project’s impacts to sage-grouse, given it “falls completely within core sage-grouse habitat” and the area holds “the only [prioritized] population which has had an increasing trend over the past 30 years, making this one of the true sage-grouse strongholds in the state.”

In a release to investors, Jindalee said it expects to begin drilling by the end of September. The release made no mention of the state-mandated conditions the company must meet first.

Supercharging a Powerful Industry

The McDermitt Caldera, an area larger than New York City with just a few hundred people living in communities along its edges, had a fiery birth roughly 16 million years ago. The volcanic hotspot below Yellowstone erupted through a number of volcanoes, one of which collapsed into its empty magma chamber. Surrounded by mountains, the basin-shaped caldera became a roughly 25-mile-long lake, and seismic activity left major deposits of mercury, uranium and lithium ore below it.

The caldera’s more recent history has been shaped by America’s approach to mining.

On federal lands—more than half of Oregon and roughly 80 percent of Nevada—the practice is governed by a Reconstruction-era law, the Mining Act of 1872. The law is one of the ways the nation incentivized white settlers to move West into lands long occupied by tribes, declaring that “all valuable mineral deposits in lands belonging to the United States” are “free and open to exploration and purchase.”

To this day, all that’s needed to stake a mining claim on public lands is to plant literal stakes in the ground, file the paperwork and pay a fee. Companies pay no royalties for the minerals extracted from the lands owned by American taxpayers, something other extractive industries, like fossil fuel developers, are required to do.

Though mines once dug by pickaxes and hauled by mules are now open pits thousands of feet deep and as wide as towns, excavated with massive vehicles and explosives, the law has not changed. It’s made mining a consistent top use of the nation’s public lands. In the McDermitt Caldera, now-closed mercury mines left behind strange-colored pools of water and piles of waste; for decades, high arsenic levels from the activity made water in the border community of McDermitt unsafe to drink.

“This is an area in which the law [and the industry built around it] is so complex there is no appetite for meaningful reform,” said Jamie Pleune, a mining-permitting expert and associate professor of law at the University of Utah’s Wallace Stegner Center. “It is very easy to conduct mineral exploration, and the law creates an entitlement that overrides other rights and concerns.”

That’s the baseline the Trump administration is supercharging, using emergency powers and recent court decisions weakening environmental laws to remake federal reviews of mineral extraction.

“Thanks to President Trump’s bold leadership, American lithium production is going to skyrocket,” U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a press release announcing the federal government’s 5 percent stake in Lithium Americas as part of a renegotiated $2.26 billion federal loan to the company.

Some of that could backfire on companies, in part through litigation.

“It doesn’t matter how fast you push your permit,” Pleune said. “If you don’t have a social license, your project is going to encounter delays, and those delays are going to cost you money.”

The McDermitt Caldera is riddled with new boreholes, evidence of noisy drilling that’s detrimental to the dwindling sage-grouse. A lithium operation here would likely pump millions of gallons of water out of a desert aquifer in an area where earlier mining harmed water quality. Environmentalists and Indigenous people fear that mining will also degrade the springs supporting the threatened trout and ancestral hunting and gathering grounds for nearby tribes, while ranchers watch mining companies lay claim to the last bit of land on which they can graze their cattle.

“When you fast track, you miss out on so much,” said Chanda Callao, an organizer with People of Red Mountain, a coalition of Fort McDermitt Paiute, Shoshone and Bannock tribal members and allies working to protect their ancestral lands in the caldera. Lithium mines threaten sacred spaces, burial grounds and places to hunt and gather traditional medicines, she said, and the companies and government “don’t inform the community of what’s happening, and [they] don’t give people that opportunity to steer the mine or to fight back against it.”

“This area is basically under siege,” said Terry Crawforth, a former director of the Nevada Department of Wildlife who lives in the area. The McDermitt Caldera is rich with wildlife, he said, especially at its northern end where Jindalee is approved to drill. “The families who have been here for 100 years farming, their kids are not going to see it.”

“If the mine goes through, I know I’m done,” said Nick Wilkinson, a local rancher whose family has lived in the area since the 1800s and whose cattle graze the land Jindalee claimed.

Wilkinson and other ranchers have worked closely with federal agencies, state officials and environmentalists to protect the Lahontan cutthroat trout—whose protections pushed ranchers off high-elevation habitat they once grazed—and sage-grouse. Jindalee’s claims are in the Wilkinson family’s low-elevation range. If that’s lost, it’s over for the ranch, Wilkinson said. There’s nowhere left for them to graze their cattle.

Before the project’s latest batch of exploratory drilling was approved, he met with Jindalee to seek a path forward. So far, he said, the company has refused to work with him. Contractors for the mine have torn up the roads and burst the water pipe for his cows three times by driving over it with heavy equipment, he said. And the mining laws allowed them to degrade the habitat he said he’s helped protect for years by maintaining area roads and fences and helping run a crew that by his count has put out roughly 30 wildfires over the past decade.

Rodger, Jindalee’s CEO, said the company is increasing its engagement with local ranchers, has supported road repairs caused by its activities and added language to its contracts with contractors “to respect private property, report and remedy damages, and operate in a manner to minimize impacts to the ongoing ranching activities.”

Wilkinson said it’s clear to him that the mine will do more harm to the sensitive species in the area than his cattle ever could. He said he’s “dumbfounded” it’s being allowed after millions of dollars in restoration work and longstanding efforts by local ranchers, and he fears he’ll lose the home where his parents are buried.

“My family’s invested their life here to create fish habitat and sage-grouse habitat and still make a living off a renewable resource,” he said. “And nobody cares. As I look back on it, I’m just like, ‘I don’t even know why I did it.’”

“White Gold in Those Hills”

Fite, of WildLands Defense, has visited the caldera regularly since 2023, documenting the wildlife and the activities of the miners while camping with her two cattle dogs—Skye and Roo.

“These days, you see odd soils and worry someone’s going to come in, saying ‘There’s white gold in those hills,’” she said as she drove her silver Toyota 4Runner to a yellow-colored hill within Jindalee’s exploration area in the caldera.

In Jindalee’s claimed area, hills made of unique clay soils support multiple sensitive wildflower species listed by the BLM, like Cooper’s goldflower and Pueblo Mountains buckwheat. Below the ridges, drilling is permitted to start soon in clearings where male sage-grouse gather for their mating dances. Pygmy rabbits nest in nearby fields rich in sagebrush. Just 200 feet away, other claims riddle streams supporting the threatened Lahontan cutthroat trout and all the rest of the local wildlife.

McDermitt Creek and its tributaries flow into Nevada’s Quinn River Valley basin. The water supply here is like a financial institution in trouble, more of its resources being withdrawn than replenished. For the last four decades, the Nevada Division of Water Resources has denied applications to pump even more groundwater from the basin. But that information, the environmental groups suing the federal government allege in their lawsuit, was omitted by the BLM as part of its approval of exploratory drilling for lithium.

The BLM’s environmental assessment noted two active sage-grouse leks in the project area and an additional 25 leks within four miles of the project’s approved drilling area. The activity will have short-term effects on the population, the BLM found, and may lead to population decline. But a seasonal shutdown and mitigation efforts post-drilling should avoid long-term issues, the agency stated. Impacts to water resources, it says, will be short term and have no effect on other users.

The disturbance of soils for the 168 drill sites will disrupt and fragment habitat and make the areas vulnerable to invasive weeds like cheatgrass, Fite said. Noise and lights will force sage-grouse to abandon leks. Since the birds return to the same lek year after year, it’s a major blow to the species when one is lost.

If the drilling finds enough lithium to make it worthwhile to dig, it will be followed by an open-pit strip mine.

“Any fool can tell you this is important sagebrush habitat,” Fite said. “There is no way to mitigate a mine out here.”

The site of Jindalee’s claims has the highest quality sage-grouse habitat designated by the state, said Skyler Vold, the conservation coordinator for the species with the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife—so good that the population has grown in recent years.

The reason for that is simple: “There’s no big human presence” in the area, Vold said. “Sage-grouse really don’t like us and our noise.”

The caldera is one of the few places with little development, few recent severe wildfires and where invasive species have not taken hold. Just drilling in the area would be a major detriment to the population, Vold said, and his agency is concerned about the project.

Oregon has a system to incentivize developers to stay away from sensitive species like the sage-grouse: If they don’t, they have to pay. During an April 2024 meeting between the state wildlife agency and Jindalee, notes taken by a contractor for the company, obtained via a records request, show those mitigation fees could “exceed $10 million.” That price “seems disproportionate” with the project’s impact, the consultant noted; the state responded that the goal is to avoid sage-grouse being placed on the endangered species list.

Jindalee has another option, though, and that’s the path it’s pursuing, according to the state. The company would purchase conservation credits through a mitigation bank program intended to provide a net benefit for the affected species and in essence replace the sage-grouse habitat lost from the drilling.

A final agreement is expected soon and could prove far cheaper than the mitigation fees. Environmentalists worry the mitigation bank will function like carbon credits: a tool that enables companies to keep harming the environment.

As Fite surveyed a patch of land near yet more mining claims with Skye and Roo, she said people don’t need to be experts to recognize the caldera is a unique and wild place. Other than the occasional miner or rancher, you could walk from the site of Jindalee’s project to Thacker Pass 20 miles south and not see a soul, she said. That’s why it’s a stronghold for many of the West’s iconic but declining species.

“This is the forgotten wildlife corridor,” she said.

Landscapes like this, she said, are the places land managers work to protect—until they’re told a mine takes precedence.

Gray clouds overhead had cleared, and water trickled down from Nevada’s Montana Mountains to a meadow of sagebrush in their foothills. The land was a lush green from recent rains, and a sea of rolling sagebrush hills surrounded Fite as she walked up a mountainside, joining the birds in song.

“Chewee, chewee, chewee, chewee,” she called out with the rock wren. “Churt, churt, churt” for the “loud-mouth” meadowlark. The long “meewww” of the spotted towhee.

On a barbed-wire fence to prevent cattle from grazing into the higher elevations, reflective markers intended to stop the sage-grouse from flying into it had faded from years in the sun.

In the valley below, more mining claims dotted the ground.

text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday he has approved that would roll back Biden-era vehicle efficiency rules, a shift he said will lower vehicle prices and give automakers more room to build the kinds of vehicles many Americans buy.

The final rule was not immediately released, and the administration has not publicly detailed the new requirements.

A prior proposal from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration would lower the fleetwide fuel-economy target for cars and light trucks to about 34.5 miles per gallon by model year 2031. That would be down from 50.4 mpg under Biden-era standards.

Trump said the change would lower vehicle prices, save families thousands on new cars and help automakers expand U.S. manufacturing. The rollback is expected to give automakers more flexibility to produce gasoline-powered pickups and SUVs, which generally have lower fuel efficiency but higher profit margins.

The Biden-era standards were designed to cut fuel use and emissions while encouraging more fuel-efficient, hybrid and electric vehicles. The rules did not require consumers to buy electric vehicles.

NHTSA previously estimated its proposed rollback could reduce the average upfront price of a new vehicle by about $930. But that proposal was also projected to increase fuel consumption by roughly 100 billion gallons through 2050, add about $185 billion in fuel costs and raise carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%.

Environmental groups criticized the move, arguing that less fuel-efficient vehicles could mean higher costs at the gas pump and more pollution.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a “major victory for America’s auto workers” was coming Monday, suggesting further details or an announcement may follow.

text:
New lithium mine in Cornwall will ramp up UK’s industrial resilience, support over 100 jobs and help make Britain better off.

Government is taking action to ensure UK has strong supply of critical mineral to back key supply chains for AI, advanced manufacturing and clean energy sectors.

Investments follows £1bn secured for UK automotive this month alone, supporting hundreds of jobs as part of the Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise Britain.

A new mine in Cornwall is set to open as the government ramps up efforts to boost industrial resilience and help secure vital supply chains backing the automotive, clean energy and advanced manufacturing sectors.

Geothermal Engineering Limited (GEL) will invest around £43 million in a new cutting-edge lithium extraction facility in Cornwall. The investment will create nearly 50 direct jobs and support around 80 more across the supply chain, after receiving an Offer in Principle worth nearly £10 million through the Government’s DRIVE35 Automotive Transformation Fund.

The move comes as demand for lithium is expected to increase by 1,100% by 2035 and will support hundreds of jobs and shore up Britain’s supplies of lithium. This critical mineral is essential for powering electric vehicle batteries, which is why the government has now taken action to unlock nearly £230 million of private investment into two lithium projects in Cornwall and Teesside.

With the UK boasting amazing natural resources, and Cornwall at the centre of one of the most important historic mining regions in both the country and Europe – this investment will help unlock the South West’s industrial potential as part of the Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise this country.

This builds on Tees Valley Lithium’s £185 million investment to establish one of Europe’s largest lithium refineries in Teesside. This investment will support hundreds of jobs and strengthen the UK’s battery supply chain, following a government Offer in Principle for £18.3 million through DRIVE35.

The investments are made possible by the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy and represent a major step forward in the UK’s transition to electric vehicles and another strong vote of confidence in Britain’s automotive sector. This is in addition to £1 billion of investment announced already this month from Bentley, McLaren and Nissan.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said:

Cornwall has a proud mining heritage, and companies like Geothermal Engineering are helping to write its next chapter in unlocking the South West’s industrial potential.

Britain isn’t just a country for innovation and ideas. It’s a country that produces, and we’re building a modern economy rooted in the industries where we’re already strong and that local communities are proud of.

Hot on the heels of over £1 billion of automotive investment secured already this month, this latest win is a big step towards building our industrial resilience.

Dr Ryan Law, CEO of GEL said:

Lithium is fundamental to the technologies underpinning the automotive sector’s transition to zero-emission vehicles. At GEL, we are proud to be at the forefront of establishing a new UK lithium industry, demonstrating how Cornwall’s geothermal brine can provide a reliable and sustainable source of this critical mineral.

We believe the UK has an important opportunity to develop the resources, technology and expertise needed to establish a domestic lithium supply, giving the country greater control over an increasingly important raw material and we are proud to be building that capability here in Cornwall, bringing jobs and new investment to the local area.

With commercial production set to begin on GEL’s Cornwall project in 2029, the facility is expected to produce around 1,500 tonnes of technical-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine underground each year – enough to power more than 180,000 typical EV car batteries.

The facility has the potential to scale to producing tens of thousands of tonnes in the future, and the lithium produced will give a huge boost to the UK’s EV battery manufacturing, shoring up crucial supply chains and moving Britain forward in the transition towards net zero.

Julian Hetherington, Automotive Transformation & Engagement Director, APC and Zenzic, said:

The project aligns with the UK’s Critical Minerals Strategy 2035 by expanding domestic production of critical minerals, reducing reliance on imports. Extracting lithium in the UK is vital for several reasons: it diminishes dependence on supply chains dominated by China and supports the production of electric vehicle batteries, essential for the UK’s transition to renewable energy use in zero emission vehicles.

In addition, the lithium extraction is expected to spark significant economic growth, especially in Cornwall where a vibrant materials cluster is developing at pace, while enhancing resilience by diversifying the supply chain and mitigating risks tied to concentrated global lithium production and processing.

Print article

Green technologies are mineral-intensive: electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and grids need cobalt, lithium, copper, manganese, graphite and rare earths. The International Energy Agency estimates that electric cars require six times more minerals than a petrol or diesel car. A wind power plant requires about nine times more minerals than a gas-fired plant.

As the global green transition speeds up, the growing demand for green technologies and minerals creates an opening for Africa, which has deposits of several of the minerals needed.

Read more: Zimbabwe's lithium is in demand for making batteries: how to make sure benefits flow to the local economy

Yet just having these minerals in the ground does not automatically create industries or shared prosperity. In fact, developing countries endowed with minerals often struggle to benefit economically from mining.

We are scholars of how countries build industries and reshape their economies. Our latest study, commissioned by the World Bank, explored how far African countries have moved beyond mining the minerals needed for the energy transition. We examined whether they are processing and refining these minerals or making components for green technologies that use them.

Our analysis followed four steps. First, we identified the transition minerals found in each African country. Second, we examined trade data to see which countries export these minerals and where they are sold.

Read more: A new class of metals could transform Africa's clean energy economy - scientists explain

Third, we looked at where African countries participate in the value chain of green technology. We wanted to find out whether they only mine the mineral and then export it raw, or whether they process it before selling it or produce a final product for sale, such as solar panels. Fourth, we reviewed national and regional mineral and industrial policies.

We found that African countries have deposits of 41 minerals that are used across bioenergy, electricity networks and infrastructure, batteries, energy storage and electric vehicles, and carbon capture and storage. These minerals are also sought after for fuel cells and hydrogen, geothermal energy, heat pumps, hydropower, nuclear power, solar power and wind power.

However, most African countries still export transition minerals in raw or lightly processed form rather than turning them into higher-value materials, components and finished products.

Read more: Has finance for green industry had an impact in Africa? What's happened in 41 countries over 20 years

African countries therefore have only a very small presence in the green-technology industries that depend on these minerals. As a result, Africa's mineral wealth has not yet led to high levels of industrial activity, well-paid jobs, higher incomes or wide improvements in living standards.

We found that national and regional institutions are taking steps to change this, but most initiatives are still at an early stage.

Our research found deposits, reserves, or production of at least one transition mineral in 48 African countries. South Africa had 24 of the 41 minerals; Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) each had 14.

Collectively, Africa holds about 96% of global platinum group metal reserves, 77% of phosphate reserves, and 55% of cobalt reserves. Phosphate and cobalt are used in electric vehicle batteries, while platinum is used in technologies that produce and use green hydrogen.

Yet most countries individually accounted for only small global shares. This matters because small national volumes can make it harder for a country acting alone to influence buyers, attract large processing plants, build complete supply chains or compete with established producers elsewhere.

Read more: DRC is the world's largest producer of cobalt - how control by local elites can shape the global battery industry

Trade data reinforces these findings. Notably, apart from South Africa, Nigeria and the DRC, most African countries exported less than 1% of each mineral globally. For several minerals, such as nickel, rare earths, silver and lithium, Africa's five largest exporters together supplied less than 10% of world exports.

African countries could strengthen their position in mineral markets by coordinating their trade policies rather than acting separately. Private companies hold mining licences, but permission to extract minerals does not always include an unrestricted right to export them. Governments may therefore have some scope to coordinate trade rules. How this would work alongside companies' existing rights, and whether it would require their agreement, needs to be further studied.

Read more: Lithium in the Sahel: how armed groups are exploiting the global scramble for the critical mineral

A deeper weakness identified in our study is limited local processing of minerals. This mainly happens in a few countries such as South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The processing these countries do often involves crushing and concentrating ore, rather than making products from the mineral.

African countries lose out because of this. For example, Congolese cobalt can sell for US$5.80 per kilogram at the point of extraction. But after local refining, the price increases to US$16.20 per kilogram, nearly tripling its value.

Asia (China in particular) is the leading importer of 16 minerals from Africa. It imported over 30% of those exports on average, and was the second biggest buyer of six other green transition minerals.

Our research found that China absorbed over 40% of Africa's annual mineral ore exports. This shows that Africa is repeating a familiar pattern: mining raw materials while other countries turn them into more valuable products.

Read more: China and the US are in a race for critical minerals. African countries need to make the rules

The history of Africa, plus low industrialisation levels, means that African countries are also almost invisible in green technology value chains. Between 2017 and 2023, Africa's global patent share across the technologies studied remained below 0.4%, while its export share was below 1% in every category. African countries currently participate in the green economy more as consumers, rather than producers.

We also found that African governments are changing mining laws, restricting exports, taking ownership stakes and forming partnerships to gain more from their minerals. They want more processing, investment, jobs and income to stay at home. Most are acting individually, although some are working together across borders.

Acting alone has limits. Many countries supply too little to influence large international buyers. If one country demands higher prices or local processing, buyers can shop elsewhere.

Many also lack reliable electricity, affordable loans, transport and skilled workers to process minerals and make components.

Africa is very strong in minerals as a continent. However, deeper regional cooperation would help African countries build industries, not simply trade more easily with one another, a central thesis of a related study, Integrating Africa: From Threads to Hubs. Pooling mineral supplies, markets, infrastructure and skills could lower costs and give them more power when negotiating with global companies. A shared processing centre serving countries across Africa would also help the continent.

Read more: Why Africa needs a green bank to fund climate action and build its own renewable technology

To make this happen, African finance and mineral institutions and national governments must agree on common priorities and similar rules about how minerals are processed, and how environmental damage is managed.

Development finance has a role to play. Regional development banks and other African financiers could help fund shared electricity, transport and mineral-processing infrastructure, while universities and businesses develop the technical skills these industries need.

Partnerships with foreign governments and companies should also go beyond extracting and exporting minerals. They should include commitments to process more minerals in Africa, share technology and know-how, train workers, and help local firms become suppliers to emerging green industries.

title: Promise seen in mixing farming, solar energy production projects | The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
description:

The cows benefit from the solar panels' shade, with researchers finding less heat stress in the herd.

In the solar garden she planted vegetables that benefit from shade: onions, collard greens, green beans and scallions.
text:
Winifred Sylvah picked a handful of plump cucumbers on a cold, wet September morning as raindrops trickled off rows of solar panels in the background.

They've been a productive plant for Sylvah on a new plot of land at a solar farm in Big Lake, Minn. She's already harvested about 140 pounds of cucumbers, with rows more waiting to be picked. Sylvah is one of three farmers working the land in between and outside the rows of a 1-megawatt solar array in Big Lake.

The Big Lake Farm is an example of agrivoltaics, a technique of mixing farming and solar power generation. The two interests are often pitted against each other in rural areas, but the rows of flourishing crops between rows of solar panels shows there's enough sun to go around.

The farm is a partnership between The Food Group -- a Minnesota-based nonprofit organization that helps emerging farmers and fights hunger -- U.S. Solar and Conexus Energy. It allows farmers like Sylvah to affordably lease farmland while providing an additional use for land that would otherwise be fenced-in rows of panels.

The project started as a pilot in 2023, but this year was made permanent with Sylvah and two other farmers entering 10-year leases on the land. She wasn't sure what to make of farming between panels, but after hearing from pilot project farmers and seeing new infrastructure like irrigation systems and a walk-in cooler to store freshly picked produce come to the land, Sylvah was up for the challenge.

"I decided to take a chance," Sylvah said.

The program expansion comes as federal officials slash support for emerging farmers. In March, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced $300 million in cuts for a grant program focused on supporting land and market access for new farmers, defunding three programs aimed at helping farmers of color in Minnesota, MPR News reported. The cuts are part of the Trump administration's eradication of federal spending aimed at diversity, equity and inclusion efforts.

"Because racial equity is a core value for our organization and how we've set up our programming, we aren't going to actively pursue federal grants for the next couple years," Food Group Executive Director Sophia Lenarz-Coy told Sahan Journal.

Accessing land is a challenge for emerging farmers. The Food Group's Big River Farms in Marine on St. Croix, Minn., is a popular incubator program for emerging farmers, many of whom are immigrants. But once they leave, farmers who can't afford to buy land often lease plots for a year at a time, which doesn't allow them the certainty to become certified organic or the chance to adapt to the soil over the years.

"What's nice about people having longer term leases is they'll have a little more time to experiment," Lenarz-Coy said.

Growing between rows of solar panels offers similar yields to standard farming, according to Iowa State University Professor Ajay Nair. Nair has helped lead research on agrivoltaics in Ames, where a partnership with utility firm Alliant Energy led to a 10-acre solar garden lined with rows of crops.

Iowa State researchers have tried various fruits and vegetables in the solar garden, and for the most part are seeing the same yield as in comparison plots.

"Any grower can commercially grow their produce within an agrivoltaic system," Nair told Sahan Journal.

There's more space between solar rows than many assume, Nair said. Wires are deep underground and typically don't prohibit tilling the land, and some plants benefit from rotating shade. As long as irrigation is in place, it's a perfectly viable place to farm, he said.

There are co-benefits between farmers and solar firms, Nair said. Solar companies build large fences around their projects, which is useful for farmers. Farmers are on the land consistently and can tell the company right away if a panel has been damaged in a storm or if anything is amiss on the property. It also helps ease rural land politics by allowing solar and agriculture to co-exist.

"Having some sort of an agriculture system in there gives them the social license to operate," Nair said.

Most agrivoltaic projects in the United States focus on livestock grazing, not produce farming. In western Minnesota, researchers at the University of Minnesota-Morris have run a successful cattle agrivoltaics plot for the past eight years.

Some 275 cows munch grass in between rows of a 500-kilowatt solar array in Morris, Minn., said animal science Professor Brad Heins. The cows benefit from the solar panels' shade, with researchers finding less heat stress in the herd. That helps keep the cows healthier and more productive, Heins said.

"I think it's garnered a lot of interest in Minnesota and around the world," Heins said.

Sylvah came to Minnesota from Sierra Leone as a student in the 1980s. She worked in banking for more than 30 years before retirement. But she always loved growing food and has fond memories of tending the family vegetable garden with her grandmother.

She grew vegetables at home and got involved in a community garden, but when she retired she decided to make farming her profession. She got involved with The Food Group and worked a plot at Big River Farms.

The Big Lake farm is much closer to her home in Otsego. And it gives her the chance to get to know the land. She has about an acre and a half total: one acre in the solar garden and half an acre in an adjacent plot.

Sylvah has a large mix of crops. In the solar garden she planted vegetables that benefit from shade: onions, collard greens, green beans and scallions. They all did well, she said.

She's learned from this season. She didn't put down fabric to discourage weeds, but she will next year after spending too much time maintaining her beds.

Her banking background shines through: Sylvah is always thinking about the market for anything she grows. She's developed a following for her West African crops. Her okra, sweet potato greens, collard greens and eggplant are in high demand, she said.

"I make sure I know people are interested in what I'm growing," Sylvah said.

She has some bitter balls, a West African eggplant that Sylvah said is popular in Minnesota's Liberian community, but she's not selling any this year and instead hopes to get seeds for a larger haul next season. In late August, she put down new rows of green beans, planning a late fall harvest.

"I always will do my last harvest for Thanksgiving," she said.

Sylvah sells her food through a Community Support Agriculture program and to local public school districts in Albertville, Minn., and Buffalo, Minn., harvesting and delivering to the schools herself this fall.
