The current occupant of the White House has not specified the concrete content of the new rules nor the planned timeline for their implementation, although he has defended that these decisions "will end the waste in automobile manufacturing in the United States."

According to Trump, the regulatory review will translate into relief for consumers: "That means lower prices, saving families thousands of dollars when buying a new, beautiful, and safe vehicle; far superior to those 'environmental monsters' that were being manufactured until now," he emphasized.

The president has also assured that "all manufacturers" have already contacted him to "express their desire" to produce on U.S. soil. "Now they can do it," he insisted, before highlighting that his Administration "is investing more than $100 billion (about €87.770 billion) in American vehicles."

"That is just the beginning. Factories are coming back, jobs are coming back to Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, South Carolina, and the rest of the country," Trump proclaimed, taking the opportunity to thank the work done by the Secretaries of Transportation and Commerce, Sean Duffy and Howard Lutnick, whom he pointed out as key pieces in this regulatory shift.

The U.S. energy storage industry has set a goal of expanding energy storage system (ESS) installations to 1 TWh (terawatt-hours) by 2032. As electricity demand rises rapidly because of AI data centers and other factors, the industry plans to use ESS to supplement insufficient power supply capacity.

The U.S. energy storage coalition (ESC) set a target of expanding the country's ESS capacity to 225 GW in output and 1 TWh in storage capacity by the end of 2032 in a recent report titled “The Opportunity of the Terawatt-Hour Era.” ESC is an industry coalition involving major U.S. grid-scale battery manufacturers, as well as ESS developers, owners and operators. One TWh equals 1,000 GWh.

The U.S. ESS market is growing rapidly. The country's energy storage capacity rose from 1.5 GW at the end of 2020 to 52 GW in mid-2026. ESC said an average annual growth rate of 25% over the next five years would be needed to expand that capacity to 225 GW by 2032.

Electricity demand in the United States is surging as AI data centers and manufacturing expand and electrification accelerates. At the same time, the growing share of renewable power generation, including solar and wind, has increased fluctuations in electricity output. ESC explained that ESS can supply stored electricity during periods of high demand, helping address peak demand and improve the utilization of the existing power grid.

ESC also projected substantial economic benefits. If U.S. ESS storage capacity expands to more than 850 GWh, electricity system costs could be reduced by more than $250 billion over the next 10 years. ESS can lower peak power costs and grid congestion while reducing the burden of additional investment in generation and transmission facilities.

As the U.S. ESS market grows, Korean battery manufacturers are moving to expand their businesses by using local production facilities. LG Energy Solution plans to use five production sites in North America as ESS manufacturing bases and expand its North American ESS production capacity to more than 50 GWh by the end of this year. Samsung SDI began mass-producing NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminum) batteries last year after converting an existing electric vehicle line at the Indiana plant of StarPlus Energy, its joint venture with Stellantis, for ESS production. It also plans to begin producing LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries in the fourth quarter of this year. SK On will convert part of its plant in State of Georgia (GA) into an LFP production line for ESS and begin mass production in the second half of the year.

President Donald Trump announced on September 26, 2026, that his administration will roll back federal fuel economy standards for automobiles, with the Transportation Department scheduled to unveil the official rule on Monday.

The policy shift targets Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards updated in 2024 under former President Joe Biden. Those regulations aimed to raise overall fleet fuel efficiency from 39.1 miles per gallon to roughly 50.4 miles per gallon by model year 2031, encouraging automakers to expand electric vehicle production.

Administration officials previously signaled a preference for lower efficiency thresholds. In December 2025, a proposal was outlined that would reduce the fleetwide requirement to roughly 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031, representing a cut of more than 30 percent from the Biden-era rule.

In a post on social media, Trump criticized the previous efficiency mandates and described the regulatory rollback as a benefit for consumers and domestic manufacturing.

"just approved new Fuel Economy Standards," said Donald Trump, President of the United States.

The president argued that the existing targets placed unnecessary financial burdens on auto manufacturers and constrained choices for buyers.

"TERMINATE," said Donald Trump, President of the United States.

He characterized the Biden-era rule as an undue government preference for electric models over petrol-powered vehicles.

"These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car," said Donald Trump, President of the United States.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the timing of the forthcoming policy release on social media.

"COMING MONDAY," said Sean Duffy, Transportation Secretary.

Though the previous administration introduced strict efficiency benchmarks, federal law does not mandate consumers to purchase electric vehicles or ban gas-powered cars. Congress also eliminated fines for carmakers failing to meet fuel standards and previously rolled back consumer tax credits for electric vehicles under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The announcement arrives as drivers face higher fuel costs across the country. According to the AAA motor club, the national average price for a gallon of gas reached $4.48 on Saturday following US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February.

text:
Korea’s planned power infrastructure investment in the United States could generate a second wave of orders for Korean battery and power equipment makers, as surging electricity consumption from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers drives demand for energy storage systems (ESS) and grid equipment.

Last week, the Korean government announced its first U.S. strategic investment project, part of a $350 billion investment package. The project worth $22.3 billion is centered on building a natural gas-fired power plant in Encinal, Texas, to meet rising electricity demand from semiconductor plants and AI data centers.

The project is also expected to create additional demand for equipment needed to store, distribute and stabilize power, enabling relevant system makers to attract more orders from the world’s largest economy.

ESS is one of the largest pillar under the project. Korean battery makers — LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On — identify ESS as their major revenue areas while the electric vehicle industry is stuck in a chasm.

ESS can store electricity when demand is low and discharge it during peak periods, helping data centers manage sharp fluctuations in power consumption and maintain a stable supply.

The need for such systems could become more pronounced around data centers that receive electricity from the new gas-fired power plant. ESS also helps stabilize power delivery between the newly built generation facilities and data centers.

Battery makers’ strategic shift toward ESS is already becoming evident.

LG Energy Solution was selected as an ESS partner for Nvidia’s AI factory program, positioning its lithium-ion phosphate (LFP)-based storage systems for AI data center applications. SK On, meanwhile, signed a 1.07 trillion won contract with POSCO Future M for LFP cathode materials, as it expands its ESS business in the U.S.

Samsung SDI is also seeing stronger demand for energy storage batteries. iM Securities expected the company’s ESS sales to rise about 32 percent in the third quarter from the previous quarter, and the firm’s sales are also projected to soar 33 percent between July and September from a year earlier on the favorable ESS market environment.

Korea’s power infrastructure investment in the U.S. could also benefit major power equipment makers here, as new power plants and data centers require transmission and distribution infrastructure, including transformers and circuit breakers.

HD Hyundai Electric, LS Electric and Hyosung Heavy Industries are among the Korean companies positioned to benefit from higher demand for high-voltage equipment. All three have expanded their U.S. orders in response to growing investment in the country’s aging power grid.

The planned investment raises expectations that Korea’s investment in U.S. power generation will lead to additional orders for Korean suppliers. As more factories and data centers are built around the project, demand for power infrastructure is widely expected to extend beyond the initial investment.

“Stable electricity storage and transmission systems are becoming inseparable parts of AI data centers,” an industry official said.

“Korea’s U.S. power investment will pave the way for such players to grab bigger orders from major Big Tech clients there.”

text:
WASHINGTON − The U.S. Transportation Department on Monday, Sept. 28 will finalize sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards through 2031, reversing a push by Joe Biden's administration to force automakers to build more electric vehicles, officials said on Sept. 26.

The new standards would cut the cost of new vehicles but increase fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, according to the department's own estimates.

President Donald Trump said he had approved new fuel economy standards for cars and trucks, which he said will lower the price of new vehicles. "A major victory for America's auto ⁠workers is coming Monday," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Trump's push comes as American drivers are grappling with sharply higher fuel prices since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran at the end of February.

He said he will lower the price of new vehicles. "A major victory for America's auto ⁠workers is coming Monday," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Under Democratic President Biden, the government sought to push automakers to build more electric vehicles to meet rising fuel efficiency standards. Biden increased required fuel efficiency for cars by 8% annually for model years 2024 and 2025, 10% for 2026 and 2% annually from 2027 to 2031.

The Trump administration ⁠in December proposed retroactively revising down the 2022 model year fuel economy standard and then raising it between 0.25% and 0.5% annually through 2031.

The Transportation Department proposed a fleetwide average of 34.5 miles per gallon by 2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon under Biden. It estimated its proposal would cut average ⁠new vehicle costs by $930 each.

But it would increase fuel consumption by around 100 billion gallons through 2050, fuel spending by $185 billion and carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%, the department said.

Trump's move will make it easier for automakers to sell ⁠consumers less efficient vehicles. "Lowering standards will accelerate what (Trump) has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump," said Pete Buttigieg, who headed the Transportation ⁠Department under Biden.

Biden focused on reducing US greenhouse gas emissions and fossil fuel use, accelerating a transition to clean energy, and making the US a global leader in clean-energy technology and manufacturing.

text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday he has approved new fuel economy standards that would roll back Biden-era vehicle efficiency rules, a shift he said will lower vehicle prices and give automakers more room to build the kinds of vehicles many Americans buy.

The final rule was not immediately released, and the administration has not publicly detailed the new requirements.

A prior proposal from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration would lower the fleetwide fuel-economy target for cars and light trucks to about 34.5 miles per gallon by model year 2031. That would be down from 50.4 mpg under Biden-era standards.

Trump said the change would lower vehicle prices, save families thousands on new cars and help automakers expand U.S. manufacturing. The rollback is expected to give automakers more flexibility to produce gasoline-powered pickups and SUVs, which generally have lower fuel efficiency but higher profit margins.

The Biden-era standards were designed to cut fuel use and emissions while encouraging more fuel-efficient, hybrid and electric vehicles. The rules did not require consumers to buy electric vehicles.

NHTSA previously estimated its proposed rollback could reduce the average upfront price of a new vehicle by about $930. But that proposal was also projected to increase fuel consumption by roughly 100 billion gallons through 2050, add about $185 billion in fuel costs and raise carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%.

Environmental groups criticized the move, arguing that less fuel-efficient vehicles could mean higher costs at the gas pump and more pollution.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a “major victory for America’s auto workers” was coming Monday, suggesting further details or an announcement may follow.

text:
And it isn’t just passenger vehicles, but also two-wheelers, three-wheelers, trucks and buses. Everything is going electric. And global geopolitics is playing a role as well.

And frankly, if we have learned any one thing from the current crisis in West Asia, it is that we cannot depend on a steady flow of crude oil or fully trust the US.

Although Donald Trump will go down in history as someone who did more to encourage electric vehicle adoption than hundreds of other politicians, with the exception of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party. Not in quite the way he intended, though.

Increasing electrification

Sales of electric vehicles have spiked in India, at a shade under 10 per cent of new car sales, and executives from Tata Motors, the country’s largest EV manufacturer, openly admit that demand far outstrips supply by almost three times. In Europe, the share of battery electric vehicles in new car registrations touched an all-time high of 27.7 per cent in August, up from 17.8 percent in the same month last year.

A trip to Europe a few weeks ago was eye-opening. Diesel prices at the pump in Germany touched the equivalent of Rs 260 per litre and recently have even hit Rs 300 per litre. India’s spare refining capacity, as highlighted by Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas Hardeep Puri at a recent conference, has played a vital role in insulating Indians from the spikes of global fuel prices. But for how much longer?

Speaking at the launch of JSW Greentech, the JSW Group’s entry into electric commercial vehicles, last week, the conglomerate’s chairman, Sajjan Jindal, highlighted the global diesel crisis and mentioned that India must move towards electrifying even heavy-duty freight and tipper trucks. Electrifying the bus fleet is, of course, low-hanging fruit. And there are huge cost benefits to electrification as well, as Parth Jindal pointed out while conversing with me during a recent conversation, with operating costs declining by almost a third on electric vehicles and margins also dramatically improving.

But as I wrote at the start of this article, noted earlier, buying an electric vehicle is a no-brainer for urban commuting. Heck, new EVs like the MG Hector Tomahawk I drove recently can easily manage over 400-450 kilometres on a single charge, so even most medium-distance highway runs are easily doable. There are still too many caveats, however.

Also read: New Mercedes GLC 400 electric is big, fast, and feature-loaded. It lacks one thing

The charging hurdle

The big caveat remains charging, particularly home charging. The crisis of charging in apartment complexes has been highlighted by automotive influencers and even in articles out here in this publication. Speaking to others Conversations across the country suggest this is not an isolated problem in Gurugram or Noida, but a nationwide issue, with Resident Welfare Associations breaking out in civil war frequently at loggerheads with local authorities, who only add fuel to the fire with various municipal and building laws regarding charging equipment being in conflict that conflict with one another.

Add to this poor electricity supply and creaking grid infrastructure in some states like Punjab and Tamil Nadu, and the ‘no-brainer’ aspect becomes one of having ‘no brain cells whatsoever’ if you go electric. Although other states like Kerala have really taken to electrification.

In fact, at the Ather Community Day, one of the more interesting services that Chief Executive Tarun Mehta announced was ‘Ather Node’, essentially a load management system (LMS). Understanding that the number of electric transformers was limited, these are the big boxes you might see that bring down the high voltage transmission to the everyday voltage we use at home. ‘Ather Node’ aimed to manage the load inside apartment complexes because, as Mehta mentioned, electric vehicles, both cars and two-wheelers, are becoming mainstream and everybody will want their own charger.

But Mehta recognised that it was unviable for an apartment complex to buy a new transformer for ₹50 lakh plus to enhance its load just because more people are buying electric vehicles. So an LMS would increase or decrease the charging rate according to the amount of spare electricity available and automate the billing process. This was not something the two-wheeler manufacturer had conceived as a profit centre; instead, they would license it out to builders and charging point operators. Mehta recognised it as a crucial investment by Ather to spread electrification.

These are not isolated issues. Other start-ups should develop LMSs, and more electrical transformers have to be made to deal with the shortage. But most importantly, the Ministry of Power and state governments will play the biggest role in this. Fixing and improving the finances of state-run power utilities and distribution companies, along with a rapid move towards renewables and energy storage, are now urgently needed to keep the blood flow of Indian mobility going.

Talking of energy storage, I’ve been reading and watching far too many videos on the latter topic, and some developments, such as mass compressed-air storage and ‘Iron-Air Batteries’, where rusting and ‘unrusting’ iron is used to store electricity, are beyond fascinating. But that is something for another column.

Kushan Mitra is an automotive journalist based in New Delhi. He tweets @kushanmitra. Views are personal.
